description: This page contains two mechanical and electrical assembly diagrams illustrating resistance spot welding configurations. Figure 2 depicts projection welding: upper and lower plates separated by a die with stamped projections, a fixed arm beneath, and a transformer connected via electrical leads to the electrode contact points. The arrangement of projections section shows different weld point configurations. Figure 3 illustrates seam welding with two revolving electrodes (rotating cylinders) mounted on opposite sides, driven by a motor connected through a transformer. Welded plates feed between the electrodes, producing either intermittent or overlapping spot welds as shown below. Both diagrams display the transformer secondary winding connections feeding current to the welding electrodes. A maintenance technician can determine the fundamental electrode configurations, mechanical feeding systems, current paths, and distinguishing characteristics between projection and seam welding processes from these schematics.

Figure 16 is a schematic diagram showing the pneumatic and electrical control circuit layout of a spot welding machine. The diagram displays a Pneumatic Cylinder connected to a Pressure Switch and Timer, which together regulate a Solenoid Operated Air Valve. The air valve drives the welding head clamping action. A Transformer with Primary and Secondary windings supplies welding current. The Foot Pedal operates an Interlock on the Main Contactor with Delayed Opening, sequencing the welding cycle. A technician can determine from this page how operator input triggers pneumatic clamping force, how the timer controls weld duration, how pressure is monitored during operation, and how the main contactor integrates pneumatic and electrical systems to coordinate safe sequenced operation of the welder. The diagram clarifies the control hierarchy and safety interlocks governing the complete welding cycle.

This page is a photograph of a pneumatically operated 40 kVA resistance spot welder manufactured by Philips. The mechanical assembly shows a vertical machine cabinet with dual air-operated cylinders mounted on opposing sides to control electrode arm pressure and positioning. At the top sits a power unit or solenoid control block with connected hose lines. The central body houses the main transformer and control circuitry. Two electrode arms extend from the upper mounting block with adjustable holder positions for clamping workpieces. A foot pedal controller with cable connection at the base allows operator activation. The manufacturer notes this machine type features pneumatic automation for timing control. A technician could assess machine capacity (40 kVA), identify the pneumatic actuation system, verify electrode arm symmetry and range, and determine whether adjustments to cylinder pressure or arm geometry are needed for different workpiece thicknesses and alloy types.

This page contains two mechanical assembly figures documenting projection welding techniques. Figure 23 is a photograph showing the dies and electrodes arrangement in a projection welding setup, with dies positioned vertically above and below the work piece, which displays a projection or raised bump feature that concentrates the weld current. Figure 24 illustrates component examples suitable for projection welding, labeled as: Projection Welded Hinge, Handle to Lid, Tubular Lamp Bracket, Copper Electrodes (shown in cross-section and side elevation), a multi-hole rectangular component with handles, Tubular Lamp Bracket and Panel (circular cross-section view), and Strap to Tubular Cass. The drawings show both orthographic projections and perspective views of parts and electrodes, enabling technicians to understand electrode geometry, work piece configuration, and typical applications for projection welding processes on sheet metal and formed components.

Mechanical assembly photographs of manually and pneumatically/hydraulically operated gun welders for resistance spot welding. Fig. 34 depicts a manually operated pinch welder using compound levers and cranks: a heavy control box connected via flexible hose to a handheld welding gun with pivoting clamping arms. Fig. 35 shows an air or hydraulically operated gun welder featuring a mushroom-shaped valve assembly atop an articulated C-frame with opposing welding electrodes and trigger actuation. The page text notes Fig. 35-42 will present various air and hydraulic welder designs applicable to sheet metal, structural steel, and heavy plate work. A technician reviewing this page would understand the transmission method from power source to welding gun, clamping arm geometry, and valve positioning for force application. No component tags, setpoints, or numeric ranges are labeled on these assembly views.

Mechanical assembly drawing showing butt seam weld tube formation stages. The page illustrates four configurations labeled Fig. 6C, Fig. 61, Fig. 62, and Fig. 63 depicting the progressive welding process for continuous tube production. The diagrams show a strip formed through six to eight stages into a tube, with two forming rollers butting the edges together beneath the tube, and welding rollers positioned above to apply heavy welding current across the butt joint. Fig. 6C shows the tube with forming rollers engaging the seam. Fig. 61 displays the formed tube cross-section and roller arrangement. Fig. 62 shows the complete tube assembly with the weld location marked. Fig. 63 provides the top view showing dual welding rollers aligned perpendicular to the seam. A technician can determine electrode positioning, seam geometry, roller alignment, and the sequence of forming and welding operations for troubleshooting joint quality issues.

This page is primarily a photograph of a complete seam welding machine assembly rather than a detailed schematic. Figure 87 shows the recommended type of seam welder mounted on a pedestal base, with a control cabinet forming the right side enclosure. The machine comprises a vertical frame supporting a motorized welding head assembly at the top with mechanical drive components, gearing, and what appears to be hydraulic cylinders for pressure control. A foot-operated control pedal is visible at the base. The assembly demonstrates the overall configuration and integration of motor drive, transmission, clamping mechanism, and welding head positioning. A technician viewing this page can understand the machine's general layout, the mounting configuration on a pedestal structure, and how the various mechanical systems are integrated into a complete production unit. No specific component labels or electrical setpoints are legible on the photograph.

This page contains Fig. 90, a photograph of a spot welder with twin electrodes, along with introductory text on practical considerations for resistance welding machine selection. The photograph shows the complete assembly: a tall vertical frame with a top-mounted welding head containing dual electrodes, mechanical clamping or feed mechanisms in the middle section, a substantial base structure, and a foot pedal control (labeled "SE") at the bottom left for operator activation. A heavy power cable extends from the unit. The accompanying text advises manufacturing engineers on factors to consider when choosing resistance welding for production assembly—specifically production volume, material thickness, available power supply, and equipment cost—and notes that most sheet metal and light-gauge metal assemblies can be successfully resistance welded. A technician could identify this machine type, understand its basic control method, and learn selection criteria for apply resistance welding to mild steel components.

This is a mechanical assembly diagram showing two electrode designs for resistance spot welding applications. Figure 109 depicts a cross-sectional view of an electrode-section assembly with annotations: electrode grooved to avoid contact between top of section and electrode, angle sufficient to avoid contact between section and electrode, amount of offset at the top, and larger tip at bottom to restrict indentation on skin, referencing the outside skin line. Figure 110 provides detailed dimensional specifications for electrode geometry, including ½" dia., 1" dia., Top Hat Section measuring ¾" width and ¼" dia. height, ⅝" dia. specification, and a larger radiused domed tip to restrict indentation on skin. Accompanying text addresses electrode contact restrictions with adjacent sections and current path considerations affecting shunting, enabling technicians to diagnose contact issues and select appropriate electrode geometry for section configurations.

Electrical schematic diagram of an ignitron seam-welder control panel showing firing voltage generation and synchronization circuits. The upper section labeled "Firing Voltage Peak Components" contains AC input transformers, rectifiers creating 400 volts DC reference, and a synchronous commutator synchronized to line frequency. The main circuit shows timing transformers TA1, TA2, TA51, TA52, TA61, vacuum tubes T4, T7, T8, and various firing components organized into left and right halves. Firing voltage sine wave components are labeled T4.51 and T4.52, with decaying DC components C7 and C3. Switches S5 and S2 control circuit paths. The right side shows output connections to the welding machine with impedance values 32-43 and 50, 57 marked. A technician can use this page to trace the complete signal path from AC mains through voltage regulation, synchronization timing, and tube firing to machine output.

Fig. 165 presents a technical reference chart for selecting electrode tip diameters in resistance spot welding of mild steel. The page displays the formula D = √t, where D is tip diameter in inches and t is the thickness of one sheet. A nonlinear graph plots electrode tip diameter D (x-axis, 0 to 5/16 inches) against metal thickness in inches (y-axis, 0 to 7/16 inches), showing the curved relationship between material thickness and required electrode size. Below the graph, a lookup table provides material thickness ranges in inches paired with corresponding electrode tip diameters, spanning from 0 to 0.009 inches thickness (1/16 inch tip) up to 0.431 to 0.517 inches thickness (3/8 inch tip). A maintenance technician can use either the formula, graph, or table to determine the correct electrode tip diameter required for a given mild steel sheet thickness, ensuring optimal weld quality and contact geometry.

This is a mechanical assembly diagram of the PS-500 double-acting spot gun used for two-sided resistance spot welding of HSS galvanized steel, mild steel, boron steel, and custom weld modes. The diagram labels six components: PS-302 C-Arm, F-44 release and weld trigger switches, weld shaft, PS-103-CM 20mm shank, PS-025 welding cap, PS-1101-CM 60mm shank, and PS-5203 clamping handle. The page also illustrates the gun's two operational states: electrode open position for part placement, and electrode closed position for welding. A technician can identify replacement parts by their part numbers, understand the gun's mechanical assembly sequence, verify correct component configuration, and learn the basic trigger operation required for initiating the welding cycle.

This mechanical assembly diagram illustrates the extension arm options available for the Pro Spot i4 resistance spot welding machine. The page displays eight extension arm models with their part designations: PS-306, PS-308, PS-305 (508mm), PS-503-W, PS-52 (Wheelhouse Arm), PS-307, PS-302 C-Arm, and PS-403 C-X Adapter. Several models are marked as optional and available through distributors. The lower section demonstrates the switching procedure with two sequential photographs: loosening the handle and pulling off the C-arm on the left, followed by inserting a new extension arm and tightening the handle on the right. A maintenance technician can use this page to identify compatible arm configurations for different welding job situations and understand the quick-disconnect procedure for swapping arms in the field. Reference is made to figure 5.3 for selecting appropriate electrodes for each arm type.

This is a mechanical assembly and alignment diagram for the PS-500 electrode holder on a resistance spot welding machine. The drawing shows the electrode alignment procedure using three adjustment screws labeled A, B, and C positioned around the electrode holder assembly. The front view depicts the copper electrode contact at center with the holding bracket. A yellow reference line indicates proper coaxial alignment. The diagram contrasts correct alignment (electrode centered, contact face parallel to work surface) versus wrong alignment (electrode tilted, creating crossed contact points marked with red X's). Instructions state that loosening screw C while tightening screws A and B moves the electrode downward. Two warning notices emphasize that improper electrode alignment results in weak, substandard welds and must be continuously maintained. Technicians can use this page to diagnose and correct alignment issues affecting weld quality.

This page from a ProSpot i4 resistance spot welding machine manual covers electrode maintenance procedures and wheel house arm assembly. Section 5.5 includes two photographs demonstrating welding electrode condition: a clean electrode versus a buildup-damaged electrode with buildup clearly shown in red. The text specifies maintaining a 6mm weld nugget diameter and references electrode cleaning with a file and periodic cap replacement. Section 5.6 is a mechanical assembly diagram showing the wheel house adapter components, labeled PS-52-5/8 (Wheel House Arm), PS-1101-CM (60mm Electrode Shank), and PS-1133-5/8 (Electrode). A technician can use this page to identify proper electrode appearance, understand when replacement is needed, and recognize the wheel house adapter assembly for accessing restricted welding locations. Safety warnings address hot electrode hazards.

Mechanical assembly diagrams showing two X-Adapter electrode configurations for the ProSpot i4 spot welder. The 90° Arm Set comprises upper electrode PS-411, lower electrode PS-412, X-Adapter PS-404, Welding Cap PS-024, Collar PS-407, Pivot Axle PS-406, and Tapered Electrode PS-405. The 45° Arm Set uses upper electrode PS-421 and lower electrode PS-422 with the same mounting structure. Both configurations share the X-Adapter accessory that enables electrode angle adjustment. The diagrams illustrate how the electrodes attach to the pivot axle through the collar assembly, with the tapered electrode shown in the 90° configuration. A technician can determine available electrode angle options, identify required replacement parts by part number, and understand the structural assembly for maintenance or reconfiguration of the spot welding arm.
This page is primarily a website landing page and marketing interface for the my.prospot.com portal rather than a technical diagram.

This page presents two calibration reference curves for the i4s resistance spot welding machine, showing the relationship between input pneumatic pressure and output clamping force. Figure 5.5 plots input pressure in psi (40 to 120 psi) against output force in both lbs (blue line: 360 to 1349 lbs) and daN (red line: 160 to 600 daN). Figure 5.6 repeats the identical data with input pressure expressed in bar (3 to 8 bar). Both curves are linear and provide labeled setpoints at each measurement interval. Above the graphs, the text describes manual weld settings accessible to administrators, including squeeze time, hold time, rise time, and fall time parameters. A technician can use these curves to verify correct output force production by referencing the input pressure at a given setpoint, or to troubleshoot force anomalies by confirming pressure calibration.

This page is a parts diagram showing electrode shank and cap component assemblies for three ProSpot welder models. PSW-080 components include: Divider P/N 90-1711, O-ring P/N 52-0086, Screw-in Shank P/N 90-1710, and Weld Cap P/N PS-023. PSW-520 components are: Divider P/N 90-1726, O-ring P/N 52-0086, Screw-in Shank P/N 90-1717, and Weld Cap P/N PS-023. PSW-WH-090 components include: Divider P/N 90-1711, O-ring P/N 52-0086, Screw-in Shank P/N 90-1723, Weld Washer P/N PS-1135, and Cap Screw M6 x 16 P/N S-103. Each assembly shows the components in exploded view. A technician could use this page to identify correct replacement parts, understand electrode assembly construction, and verify proper component compatibility for their specific welder model.

Pneumatic air-supply connection and adjustment procedures for a resistance spot welding machine. The page shows two main sections: "Connecting Compressed Air" and "Supplying Compressed Air." The connecting section illustrates a female coupler (Nitto Koki 40SH) with 3/8" primary rubber hose connection. The supplying section provides step-by-step adjustment instructions using an adjusting knob on a regulator assembly with a pressure gauge. Key setpoint is 0.5 MPa (71 psi). The instructions direct technicians to pull the adjusting knob until an orange line appears, then turn the knob clockwise to increase or counterclockwise to decrease air pressure until the gauge reads the target 0.5 MPa, then push the knob in to make the orange line disappear. A warning notice advises cleaning new metal piping before connecting to remove foreign matter that could cause operational trouble.

This mechanical assembly diagram illustrates the foot switch unit for a resistance spot welding machine, depicting the UPPER ELECTRODE and LOWER ELECTRODE with their operational positions and movements. The drawing shows three distinct states: RETRACT POSITION, WELDING STANDBY POSITION, and WELDING POSITION, with labeled stroke measurements in mm (inches): 75 (2.95), 50 (1.97), and 25 (0.98). The UP FOOT SWITCH and DOWN FOOT SWITCH control electrode motion: pressing the DOWN FOOT SWITCH moves the upper electrode from standby to welding position; pressing the UP FOOT SWITCH retracts it 50 mm (1.97 in.) from standby position. The diagram includes RETRACT STROKE and WELDING STROKE segments. A critical note specifies the maximum welding standby position must not exceed 25 mm (1 in.) from the lower electrode. A technician can use this page to verify electrode stroke lengths, adjust standby positioning, and understand the complete operational sequence of the foot-controlled welding machine.

Troubleshooting reference table for resistance spot welding defect correction from Spot Weld, Inc. The table maps five common weld defects to their recommended corrections. Defect types listed are: Insufficient strength, Spatter generation, Workpiece sticking to electrode, Explosive spatter generation, and Dent or burn. Corrections involve adjusting three primary parameters: electrode force, weld time, and welding current. Specific adjustments include dressing the electrode tip, cleaning workpiece surfaces, and checking gap alignment between upper and lower electrode tips. A technician can use this page to identify weld quality problems and determine which process parameters to modify. The document lists the manufacturer's contact information and product categories including resistance welding equipment, electrodes, tooling, and stud welding systems. No numeric setpoints or ranges are specified; corrections are qualitative parameter adjustments.

Daily maintenance checklist for a Spot Weld, Inc. resistance spot welding machine. The page lists required machine inspections performed every day for safe, trouble-free operation. Checks include abnormal vibration, noise, and odor; air pressure verification at 0.5 MPa (71 psi); air filter drain condition; abnormal overheating; power cable damage; and water leakage at the machine and electrode cooling water hose connections. A small mechanical diagram illustrates the air filter assembly with a white button located at the lower part of the filter housing for drain removal. A maintenance technician can use this page to identify critical daily inspection points, verify pneumatic system pressure within specification, confirm air filtration system integrity, and detect early signs of cooling system failures or electrical hazards before they cause equipment downtime or safety incidents.

This is a mechanical assembly and maintenance instruction diagram for changing electrode tips on a Spot Weld, Inc. resistance spot welding machine. It illustrates foot switch controls—UP FOOT SWITCH and DOWN FOOT SWITCH—that position the upper electrode through key states including WELDING STANDBY POSITION and RETRACT POSITION. The electrode assembly comprises TIPS and TIP HOLDERS. Step two provides electrode removal procedures: apply a wrench to the upper electrode tip and strike vertically with a plastic hammer. A critical NOTICE warns against forcibly removing the tip with a wrench or similar tool, as this damages the taper portion of the tip or tip holder. A technician can determine proper tool sequence, correct electrode positioning, safe removal techniques, and damage prevention methods from this page.

This cooling water circuit diagram shows the TIP HOLDER assembly and heat-resistant tube configuration for a resistance spot welding machine. The diagram depicts proper placement of the HEAT-RESISTANT TUBE (OD: 8 mm, ID: 6 mm) positioned to direct cooling water flow to the TIP COOLING WATER FLOW PATH. Step 3 notes that if the heat-resistant tube end is not positioned close enough to the cooling water flow path of the tip, insufficient circulation occurs, resulting in improper welds. For longer tips, technicians must extend the heat-resistant tube to ensure adequate water circulation. Step 4 illustrates an alternative arrangement showing components including a smaller HEAT-RESISTANT TUBE (OD: 6 mm, ID: 4 mm). A maintenance technician can use this page to verify proper cooling tube sizing, confirm correct tube positioning relative to water flow paths, and determine when tube extensions are necessary to maintain welding quality.

Maintenance procedure page for resistance spot welding equipment, featuring two illustrated sequences. The upper section covers changing the tip holder, showing cooling water inlet and outlet connections on an arm cap (32mm outside diameter), with steps to loosen socket head bolts and remove the tip holder for replacement. A note emphasizes connecting the cooling water hose for proper operation. The lower section addresses centering electrode holders after electrode change, using a ruler to verify alignment with the upper and lower electrode holders by loosening arm bolts. These procedures are essential for maintaining proper thermal cooling flow and electrode alignment, directly affecting weld quality and equipment performance.

This is a pneumatic piping drawing depicting the complete air circuit for a resistance spot welding machine. The diagram shows two main assemblies with circled component reference points connected by solid and dashed lines representing air supply, signal, and return paths. The upper section illustrates the central pneumatic valve manifold block with solenoid-operated directional control valves, pressure regulation, and gauge provisions. The lower section shows electrode holder actuation cylinders and welding head positioning mechanisms. Components include solenoid valves, air cylinders, pressure regulators, check valves, needle valves for flow control, and gauge blocks. A technician can use this drawing to trace pneumatic logic sequences during operation, verify proper air routing to weld head clamps and electrode positioning cylinders, identify pressure setpoint locations, and diagnose system malfunctions by following signal flow from pilot air sources through control valves to work cylinders and exhaust ports.

This is a cooling water system circuit diagram for a Spot Weld, Inc. resistance spot welding machine, depicting the complete coolant circulation path. The circuit originates at the water tank and flows through a radiator, chiller unit, and pump (labeled position 1) before distributing to the spot welder machine. The system uses color-coded lines—RED and GREEN—to distinguish separate cooling loops, with numbered nodes (1 through 13) marking connection points and measurement locations. Key components include the inverter control unit, transformer, diode, upper and lower electrodes, and upper and lower arms. A caution note specifies that hoses extending to the electrode holder must be long enough and secured with bands to prevent interference. Technicians use this diagram to trace coolant flow paths, identify leak points, verify proper circuit connections, diagnose temperature distribution issues, and understand how cooling reaches the welding electrodes during operation.

Model 108 Weld Control Form from Spot Weld, Inc., a data entry sheet for recording resistance spot welding parameters and specifications. The form captures job identification (Job #, Date, Group, Weld Schedule #), welding cycle timing parameters (Squeeze Delay, Squeeze Time, Impulse, Cool Time, Heat Time, Heat %, Quench Time, Temper Time, Temper %, Hold Time, Off Time), and material specifications (Material 1 Type, Thickness, Material 2 Type, Thickness). It includes electrode configuration (Transformer #, Transformer Tap), manual valve settings (Manual Valves *9 with five numbered positions, Valve Mode), control mode selection (*1, *2, None with Chained Successive options), and pressure settings (Upper Tip Material and Size, Lower Tip Material and Size, Electrode Pressure, Clamp Pressure, Upset Pressure). A comments section at the bottom allows additional notes. Technicians use this form to document and standardize weld control settings for repeatable welding operations.

Instructional page with mechanical assembly diagrams and setup guidance for rocker arm spot welders. The page explains rocker arm mechanics through teeter-totter analogy and operational illustration. It emphasizes that upper electrode approaches material in an arc during the rocking motion. Six alignment diagrams compare proper and improper arm configurations, labeled OK and NO, showing electrode parallelism and angular orientation ("clocking"). The diagrams demonstrate that misaligned or non-parallel arms, whether tilted forward, backward, or at angles, result in poor weld quality. A technician can use this page to troubleshoot weld defects by checking arm parallelism and rotation orientation, ensuring upper and lower arms are parallel to each other and properly positioned. The page answers: how should rocker arm electrodes be aligned, what causes quality problems in rocker arm welders, how to identify setup faults.

This is an electrical wiring schematic diagram (section 2.5.1) for the resistance spot welding machine's control and power distribution system. The diagram shows a multi-line power distribution layout with control circuits on the left side and main power circuits extending rightward. Visible component labels include S1 (main switch), CN1 (connector), MSW (main switch relay), and RFF (likely a transformer or contactor mounted on the right). The left portion contains a user interface panel with multiple switches and relays controlling the welding sequence. Horizontal lines represent power rails carrying alternating current to the welding transformer shown on the right side. Vertical connections link control circuits to power switching elements. The schematic allows technicians to trace signal paths during troubleshooting, identify correct wire routing during assembly, and verify proper electrical connections between the control panel, main power distribution, and the welding electrode circuit. Grid references along the borders enable locating specific circuit elements.

This electrical schematic diagram shows the control wiring for a resistance spot welding machine. Components include FU1 and FU2 (fuses), MSY (solenoid), TRF (transformer), REL (relay), and S1 (main switch). A "USER SIDE AIDE" terminal box appears on the left with multiple connection points. The main power distribution flows from the transformer through control relays and solenoids. On the right side is a specification and legend block containing voltage ratings and operational parameters. The center section contains logic circuits with multiple signal paths controlling welding operations. Various numbered terminals and junction points indicate connection locations throughout the system. A technician could use this diagram to verify proper electrical connections, trace signal paths during troubleshooting, identify component locations, and confirm voltage distribution to welding coils and control circuits.

Electrical wiring schematic for the user-side control circuitry of a resistance spot welding machine. Three-phase AC power (L1, L2, L3) feeds through transformer TRF and main contactor MSA to control modules PX500 and PX150P. Connector CN1 links the user interface to the control logic. The diagram shows relay contacts, solenoid driver circuits (marked with spring symbols), diodes, and numbered switch connections (EB1–EB6, EX elements) routing control signals through the circuit. Multiple safety and control interlocks are visible throughout. A maintenance technician can use this to trace signal flow paths during operation, verify relay pull-in and dropout sequences, check switch continuity for proper control function, understand the weld-cycle control logic, and systematically troubleshoot failures in the control chain from user input through solenoid activation.

Electrical control schematic for a resistance spot welding machine showing power distribution and control logic. The diagram includes main input power connections (left side) with transformer TRF, control relays and contactors, timer circuits, and a protective module labeled 680EC1B. Key components visible include CN1 connector, MSW (main switch), multiple relay coils marked with numbered designations, and switching logic controlling welding sequence and safety functions. Signal paths show connections between pressure switches (PXP designations), control inputs, and output actuation of welding electrodes. The schematic enables a technician to verify proper power supply routing to the transformer, confirm control interlock logic, trace signal flow through relays and timers that govern weld duration and force application, identify protection device setpoints, and diagnose electrical faults in the control chain. Manual annotations reference multiple terminal connections throughout the circuit.

Section 2.6 pneumatic diagram for a Sureweld resistance spot welding machine. This schematic depicts the compressed air circuit architecture with four primary components: C1, a multi-port air supply valve on the left; EV1, a solenoid-actuated directional control valve with numbered ports 2, 3, 4, and 5 controlling air flow direction; FR-M, a regulator-filter assembly in the center managing pressure and filtration; and VS-R, a solenoid valve on the right terminating the circuit. Air flows left to right, with EV1 serving as the main directional control and FR-M providing pressure regulation downstream. A technician can use this diagram to trace pneumatic signal paths, identify pressure drop points, locate solenoid actuation control nodes, troubleshoot air leaks between junction points, and understand the sequence of air distribution to the welding gun pneumatic actuators.

PCB jumper configuration reference table for a Resistance Welding Solutions spot welder. The document lists three jumper locations and their functional states. JP7 controls the internal firing circuit—positioned closed to enable it, open to disable it. JP8-JP9 are parallel jumpers that control the internal supply transformer, also with closed position enabling and open position disabling the transformer. A technician can use this table to quickly determine which jumper positions are required for their welding machine configuration, either enabling or disabling the firing circuit and transformer subsystems based on machine requirements. This reference supports troubleshooting and system configuration during setup or maintenance procedures.
